topics.title: Health, Wellness, Illness & Social Determinants
topics.summary: Health is personal and keeps changing. Assess the whole person, including daily-life barriers, before you decide what wellness should look like.
objectives: You can tell health, wellness, disease, illness, and injury apart.
You can use the nine wellness dimensions to find strengths and concerns.
You can compare acute illness, chronic illness, remission, relapse, and exacerbation.
You can link the five social determinant areas to real nursing actions.
You can explain how illness changes family roles and caregiving.
You can spot when a chronic illness has a new, urgent change.
topics.bigPicture:
Two clients can have the same diagnosis and very different lives. One person with diabetes may feel capable, connected, and happy. Another person with no disease may feel tired, alone, and unsafe at home. A diagnosis matters, but it does not describe the whole person.

This lesson gives you a way to ask what matters to the client. It also helps you see what makes healthy choices possible, such as money, transport, and support. Nurses treat today’s problems, protect function, and help people reach their own goals. Wellness is still possible with chronic disease or disability.
recap: Health is a moving picture on a continuum, not a fixed label.
Disease is a body problem. Illness is how the person feels and lives it.
Wellness has nine dimensions and is possible during chronic illness.
Acute describes the course of an illness, not how severe it is.
Remission is not cure. A chronic illness can have an acute exacerbation.
A new change from baseline comes first, even in long-term disease.
Missed care is a cue to assess barriers, not proof the client does not care.
Willingness is not ability. Assess what the caregiver can safely do.

keyTerms.def: Complete physical, mental, and social well-being, not just the absence of disease (WHO, 1948). It is personal and changes over time.
A self-directed, evolving process toward well-being. It has nine dimensions.
How satisfied, purposeful, and emotionally well a person feels. A lab result cannot measure it.
A range from optimal wellness to illness to severe illness. No clear line separates health from illness.
A change in body structure or function from infection, trauma, genetics, or other factors. It can exist without illness.
The person’s own experience of feeling unwell. It can affect any wellness dimension.
An act or event that causes damage or loss of body function. It can be intentional or unintentional.
Illness with a sudden onset and short duration. Symptoms range from mild to severe.
Illness that lasts 3 months or longer. It is often lifelong and may not be curable.
Symptoms disappear. It does not always mean the disease is cured.
The disease returns after a remission.
A sudden worsening, or flare-up, of a condition the person already has.
Conditions where people live, learn, work, play, and worship that shape their health and chances.
A gap in illness, injury, disability, or death rates among groups, caused by barriers to meeting wellness needs.
The client explains or shows the teaching in their own words, so the nurse can check understanding.

sections.heading: What does being healthy mean?
sections.keyIdea: Health is personal and changes over time, so ask each client what being healthy means to them.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 3–5, 8–9
sections.body:
The WHO (1948) defines health as complete physical, mental, and social well-being, not just the absence of disease. The course adds that health is personal and changes over time. Life experiences, expectations, age, and culture all shape it.

The health-illness continuum runs from optimal wellness, to illness, to severe illness. Health is relative and always changing. No clear line separates health from illness. People move back and forth along the line.

Perception matters. A client may see their health differently than others do. A person with a chronic condition can still sleep better, move more, or feel more connected. The continuum is a useful tool for setting goals with the client.

Ask, “What does being healthy mean to you?” and “What would you most like to be able to do?” Answers like going back to work or caring for a grandchild connect your plan to real life. This is how health promotion begins: by understanding the person’s own view.
sections.analogy: A diagnosis is one photograph. The health-illness continuum is a movie. It shows symptoms, function, relationships, and resources changing over time.
bullets: Well-being (CDC, 2018): positive emotions, such as happiness and contentment.
Absence of negative emotions, such as depression and anxiety.
Life satisfaction, fulfillment, and positive functioning.
It is promoted by good health, relationships, resilience, and access to resources.
It is not set by health status alone. A normal lab value cannot measure it.

sections.heading: What are the nine wellness dimensions?
sections.keyIdea: Wellness is a self-directed, changing process with nine dimensions that affect each other, so a strength in one can help another.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 6–7
sections.body:
Wellness is a self-directed, evolving process toward well-being. It is multidimensional and holistic. Daily choices about food, activity, relationships, and rest affect it. Positive life events add to it.

The course lists nine dimensions. Together they shape total well-being. They work like gears. Stress in one area often spreads to others. Money stress can lead to missed medicine, extra shifts, poor sleep, and less time with friends.

Look for strengths, not only problems. A reliable friend might drive the client to visits. A creative hobby may help someone cope with a new disability.
bullets: Physical: healthy behaviors, activity, rest, and nutrition.
Emotional: understanding and expressing feelings.
Financial: managing money and planning for the future.
Intellectual: lifelong learning and critical thinking.
Career: meaning and satisfaction in work.
Social: supportive, respectful relationships.
Creative: expressing yourself through art and culture.
Environmental: caring for your surroundings and community.
Spiritual: connecting to purpose and meaning. Religion is not required.

rows: How are your energy, sleep, and mood?
Does work or cost make your care hard?
What do you enjoy learning or making?
Who supports you? What gives you meaning?
How are your home and community surroundings?

sections.heading: Disease, illness, and injury: how do they differ?
sections.keyIdea: Disease is a change in the body, illness is the person’s experience of feeling unwell, and injury is damage from an act or event.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 12, 14
sections.body:
Disease is a change in body structure or function. Causes include infection, trauma, genetics, or other factors. Illness is the personal experience of feeling unwell. It can affect any dimension of wellness.

The two do not always match. People may feel ill without disease, or have disease without illness. A client with high blood pressure may feel fine. Learn how each client defines and experiences illness. Do not dismiss symptoms because one test was normal.

Injury is an act or event that causes damage or loss of body function. It can lead to acute or chronic illness. Injuries can be intentional or unintentional. Both can cause trauma or disability.

Prevention includes using PPE, warming up before activity, and following safety rules. Ask about work, home, and activity without blame.

rows: Body structure or function has changed
BP 152/96 at three visits, but the client “feels fine”
Fatigue and joint aches with normal first labs
Damage or loss of function from an act or event
Hip fracture from a fall; hearing loss from years of loud noise

bullets: Noise exposure → hearing loss
Puncture wound → tetanus
Asbestos inhalation → chronic lung disease

sections.heading: Acute or chronic: what is the difference?
sections.keyIdea: Acute means sudden onset and short duration; chronic means 3 months or longer. Neither word tells you how severe the illness is right now.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 13, 19
sections.body:
Acute illness has a sudden onset and short duration. Symptoms range from mild to severe. It may resolve, or it may need urgent care. Examples are pneumonia and meningitis.

Chronic illness lasts 3 months or longer. It is often lifelong and may not be curable. Common examples are heart disease, diabetes, COPD, chronic kidney disease, cancer, and Alzheimer’s disease. Some other sources use different time rules, but use 3 months for this course.

A chronic illness can still change suddenly. Do not assume “chronic” means stable or “acute” means severe. Look at current findings and the change from baseline.

One illness touches many nursing concepts. The course example is a client with COPD. Low oxygen can cause confusion. Oxygen plus smoking is a safety risk. Poor intake upsets fluids. Limited mobility affects independence. Caregivers may feel fatigue and fear.
bullets: Remission: symptoms disappear. It is not always a cure, so follow-up still matters.
Relapse: the disease returns.
Exacerbation: a sudden worsening, or flare-up.
sections.example: A client with COPD usually dresses alone. Today he stops for breath after every few words. His daughter says, “It’s just his lung disease.” This is a new change from baseline, an exacerbation. Assess his breathing now.

sections.heading: What are social determinants of health?
sections.keyIdea: Social determinants are the conditions where people live, work, learn, play, and worship. They decide whether a care plan is even possible.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 10–11
sections.body:
Social determinants of health (SDOH) are the conditions in which people live, work, learn, play, and worship. They affect health, well-being, and quality of life. They include access to safety, housing, food, education, and health care. Nurses assess these environments to understand what shapes a client’s health.

A missed visit may mean no bus or no childcare. Ask concrete, neutral questions. “How do you get to appointments?” “Have you had trouble getting enough food?” Explain why you ask, and protect privacy. Then match each barrier to a resource, such as social work or a low-cost pharmacy program.
bullets: Economic stability: employment, income, childcare, and basic needs.
Neighborhood and built environment: safe housing, clean air and water, and freedom from violence.
Health care access and quality: culturally competent, affordable, evidence-based care.
Social and community context: support systems, recreation, discrimination, and isolation.
Education access and quality: quality schooling, technology access, and literacy.

rows: Coordinate safe storage and a workable plan
Use plain words, pictures, few key points, and teach-back
Find a safe activity option together
Says past clinics treated them badly
Listen and validate first, then advocate for respectful care
Ask about support and connect to community resources

sections.heading: What are health disparities?
sections.keyIdea: Health disparities are gaps in illness, injury, disability, or death rates between groups. They come from barriers and unequal access, not from the group itself.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 16–17
sections.body:
Health disparities are gaps in illness, injury, disability, or mortality rates among groups. They are caused by barriers to meeting wellness needs. They result from limited access to resources and care, which are the social determinants.

Preventing them requires fair access to education, food, housing, health care, and clean environments. At the bedside, assess each client’s conditions and access. Do not use stereotypes about a group.
bullets: Race or ethnicity
Sex or gender identity
Disability status
Socioeconomic status
Age or geographic location

rows: Lack of running water or electricity → higher rates of diabetes, liver disease, and injuries
Higher rates of suicide, violence, discrimination, and substance use
Children exposed to secondhand smoke → more asthma, infections, and SIDS risk
3–4 times higher maternal mortality; more gestational diabetes and preterm birth. Linked to racism, bias, and unequal access to care.

sections.heading: How does illness affect the family?
sections.keyIdea: Illness affects the whole family, so assess coping and roles, and check what helpers can truly do.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 15; caregiver and privacy points added for the NCLEX
sections.body:
Illness can affect daily life: work, rest, self-care, and relationships. Illness behavior is how a person identifies, interprets, and responds to symptoms. Chronic illness may bring grief, fear, anxiety, or loss of control. Disability requires adaptation and emotional adjustment.

Family dynamics often shift. A person who cared for everyone may now need help bathing. A teen may take over housework. The nurse assesses coping, supports adaptation, and strengthens family function.

Ask the client who they consider family and who they want involved. An alert client decides who receives their health information.

Willingness does not prove ability. A spouse who says, “I’ll do everything,” may have back pain or work nights. Watch them practice. Support the client’s own roles, because doing everything for them can increase feelings of uselessness.
bullets: Ask, “What has changed at home?”
Ask, “Who can help, and what can they actually do?”
Watch a return demonstration of any hands-on skill.
Offer practice, respite resources, equipment, or referral as needed.
If help at home cannot meet the client’s needs, escalate before discharge.

sections.heading: How do I turn assessment into a plan?
sections.keyIdea: Use ADPIE: gather subjective and objective data, name problems, risks, and strengths, plan with the client, then check whether the barrier was removed.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 18, 32–37
sections.body:
Nurses promote wellness in every care setting. Inpatient care needs a hospital admission. Outpatient care happens without a hospital stay, as in clinics. Community care happens outside the hospital, such as at home, school, or public health.

Assess. Subjective data are what the client shares: history, beliefs, and symptoms. Objective data are what you observe: exam, vital signs, and mental status. Cover the chief concern, health, family, and social history, lifestyle habits, and SDOH.

Diagnose. Name problems (current needs), risks (potential illness or injury), and wellness strengths (readiness and motivation for change). One client can have all three.

Plan, implement, evaluate. Plan with the client and the interprofessional team. Write a measurable goal. Evaluate by reassessing progress and adjusting the plan. A referral is an action. The outcome is the barrier removed.
steps: Ask what matters most to the client.
Find the problems, risks, and strengths.
Match each barrier to a practical resource.
Set a measurable goal with the client.
Check the result and revise if needed.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Most wrong answers blame the client, trust a label, or skip a new change from baseline.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 9, 12–13, 15, 37; rows on adherence and caregivers added for the NCLEX
sections.body: These look-alike ideas cause many missed questions. Learn how to tell them apart.

rows: Disease is the body change. Illness is the person’s experience. One can exist without the other.
Acute means sudden and short. It can be mild or deadly.
Chronic means long-lasting. It can still flare suddenly.
Remission means symptoms disappear. The disease can still return (relapse), so follow-up continues.
Missed care often comes from cost, transport, or literacy. Assess first.
A willing helper may lack strength, time, or skill. Verify.
New confusion is a change from baseline. Assess it right away.
A referral is an action. The outcome is the barrier removed.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Pick the answer that assesses barriers or new changes first, respects the client, and fits real life.
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials
sections.body:
Questions often give a label like “nonadherent” or “just his disease.” They test whether you look past it. Others ask you to sort clients by priority. A sudden change in a chronic illness usually wins over a stable resource need.

Here is a sample question. A client with diabetes missed two clinic visits. The client says, “I want to stay healthy, but I cannot keep doing this.” The chart says “nonadherent.” What should the nurse do first?
bullets: Common patterns: “what should the nurse do first,” “which finding needs follow-up,” and select-all barrier lists.
Priority questions mix an acute flare with stable wellness or access needs.
Hopeless statements, like “I don’t see the point,” need a direct question about suicide first.
steps: Read the stem: missed visits, a wish to stay healthy, and a label of nonadherence.
What is it really asking? Will you assess the reason or accept the label?
Key cues: “I want to stay healthy” is a strength. “I cannot keep doing this” hints at a barrier.
Wrong options: Reviewing complications assumes a knowledge gap. Having a caregiver schedule visits takes over before you know the problem. Phone reminders assume the client simply forgets.
The answer: Ask what is making it hard to get to visits, such as transport, cost, or work.
Strategy: When a client misses care, assess the barrier before you teach or judge.

sections.heading: Worked case: a plan that fails at home
sections.keyIdea: When a plan fails at home, find the real barriers and change the plan, not just the teaching.
sections.source: Added: worked example based on Module 7 slides 10–11, 33–37
sections.body:
Ms. R has stable diabetes. She wants to avoid another hospital stay. She can explain her medicines. Yet she has missed visits and buys cheap food that differs from her meal plan.

She cares for two grandchildren and rides the bus. These cues do not mean she lacks interest or knowledge. Her wish to stay well is a strength. Her clear explanation shows some understanding.

Transport, food cost, and caregiving are likely social determinants. Several barriers may be working together. Ask about each one. Keep checking her symptoms and safety, too.
steps: Name her strengths: she wants to stay well and knows her medicines.
Ask about each barrier: bus times, school pickup, and food money.
Match barriers to help: a new visit time, transport options, and affordable food resources.
Set a measurable goal, such as attending the next visit using the new plan.
Evaluate: did she get there, and can her household follow the plan?

check.q: Why is “teach the same plan again” not enough for Ms. R?
check.a: She already shows knowledge. Transport, cost, and caregiving may block action. More teaching cannot create money or time, so change the practical plan.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.source: Module 7 slides 2–37 (course notes and clarifications)
sections.body: Use these notes to connect the lesson with your course materials.
bullets: Source: Module 7 – Health, Wellness, Injury, Illness + Exemplars, slides 2–37.
Bedside examples, caregiver points, and NCLEX strategy are added to help you apply the slides.
The slides define chronic illness as lasting 3 months or longer. Some other sources use other time rules. Use 3 months for this course.
The disparity examples are the slide’s data. Use them to look for barriers, not to stereotype a client.

pearls: A diagnosis does not show how well a person functions or how they define wellness.
A chronic illness can flare. Prioritize the new change from baseline.
Assess resource barriers before blaming missed care on motivation.
Address health disparities by looking at access and conditions, not stereotypes.
Treat the urgent body problem first, then the social barrier that caused it.
An alert client chooses who counts as family and who gets information.
redFlags: New severe symptoms or fast loss of function need prompt assessment, even with a long-term diagnosis.
New confusion is never “just aging.” Compare with baseline and assess right away.
Hopeless statements, like “I don’t see the point anymore,” need a direct suicide-risk question.
Caregiver exhaustion, or no food, shelter, or medicine, can make a discharge plan unsafe.

checks.q: A client has had a blood pressure of 152/96 at three visits but says, “I feel fine, so I can’t have a disease.” How should the nurse respond?
checks.a: Explain that disease can be present without illness. High blood pressure often has no symptoms, so feeling well does not rule it out.

checks.q: A client misses visits because the bus route ended. What should the nurse assess?
checks.a: Transportation and access to care. Work with the client on a realistic option before assuming unwillingness.

checks.q: A client in remission from lymphoma plans to cancel all follow-up visits. What is the best response?
checks.a: Explain that remission is not the same as cure. Follow-up visits help find a relapse early.

checks.q: A home health client with Parkinson disease for 10 years has a new fall and new trouble swallowing. Is this “just the disease”?
checks.a: No. New changes from baseline in a chronic illness need prompt follow-up and assessment.

checks.q: An insulin user is skipping doses to save money and now has a glucose of 348 mg/dL with nausea. What comes first?
checks.a: Address the high glucose and symptoms first. Then work on the cost barrier with social work or pharmacy resources.

topics.title: Prevention, Health Beliefs & Behavior Change
topics.summary: Pick the prevention level by its purpose, match your approach to the client’s readiness, and build a plan the client can really carry out.
objectives: You can sort actions into primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention.
You can separate modifiable risk factors from ones that cannot change.
You can name a client’s stage of change from what they say.
You can respond to beliefs, locus of control, and low confidence.
You can write a measurable SMART-EST goal and revise it after a relapse.
You can respond safely when a client uses supplements or alternative care.
topics.bigPicture:
Health promotion helps people feel and function better. Prevention lowers the chance, severity, or harm of illness and injury. The two overlap. Teaching safe walking can build confidence and also prevent falls.

A perfect teaching sheet is useless if the goal does not matter to the client, the timing is wrong, or resources are missing. So the nurse starts by listening. Think of behavior change as a partnership. The client brings priorities and life experience. The nurse brings knowledge, support, and follow-up.
recap: Primary prevents disease before it occurs. Secondary detects and treats it early. Tertiary restores health and reduces impact.
Classify prevention by purpose and timing, not by whether the nurse is teaching.
Modifiable means changeable, not easy. Family history does not cancel lifestyle benefits.
Match your words to the stage of change. Explore beliefs before offering a plan.
Planning a change is preparation. Doing it is action.
Relapse is common and expected. Explore the trigger and revise the plan together.
Good goals name an observable behavior, amount, time frame, and review date.
Ask about supplements without judgment, and coordinate review. Never stop therapy on your own.

keyTerms.def: Supporting and encouraging wellness at the individual, family, community, and population level.
Promoting health and preventing disease before it occurs. Examples: vaccines, helmets.
Detecting and treating disease early, such as by screening people with no known diagnosis.
Restoring health and reducing the impact of a disease that already exists, such as rehab after a stroke.
A risk that can change, such as inactivity, poor diet, tobacco, alcohol, or lack of sleep.
A risk that cannot change, such as age, family history, or ethnicity.
Internal: belief that one can influence health outcomes. External: belief that outside factors control health.
A person’s belief that they can succeed at a specific action.
How willing and prepared a person is right now to change a behavior.
Slipping back into an old behavior during change. The course says it is common and expected, not failure.
A goal that is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound, evidence-based, strategic, and tailored.
Nontraditional care blended with conventional treatment, such as yoga, meditation, massage, or acupuncture.
A practice used instead of conventional medicine. It is rare.
Care that combines evidence-based medicine and wellness practices, focusing on mind, body, and spirit.
How people see themselves, including self-esteem, body image, roles, and abilities.

sections.heading: What are the three levels of prevention?
sections.keyIdea: Primary prevents disease before it occurs, secondary detects and treats it early, and tertiary restores health and reduces the impact of existing disease.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 22
sections.body:
The goal of prevention is to shift from treating disease to promoting wellness and preventing illness. Prevention happens at three levels. Nurses play a key role at each level through education, screening, and care coordination.

Primary prevention promotes health and prevents disease before it occurs. Vaccines and helmets are classic examples.

Secondary prevention detects and treats disease early. Screening is the key word. A blood pressure check for an adult with no known diagnosis is secondary.

Tertiary prevention restores health and reduces the impact of chronic disease. Rehab after a stroke is tertiary.

The same action can fit different levels. Teaching shows up at all three levels. So “the nurse teaches” does not automatically mean primary. Ask: has the condition already happened?

rows: Balance class for older adults who have never fallen
Vision screening for a teen with no known problem
Teaching monthly skin self-exams to an adult with no skin cancer
Restore health; reduce impact of existing disease
Energy conservation teaching for a client with COPD

sections.example: A student says a balance class for adults who never fell is secondary “because they are high risk.” Correct the student. No fall has happened yet, so the class is primary prevention.

sections.heading: How do national goals and populations guide care?
sections.keyIdea: National goals guide population health, but each client and population group still needs care that fits their age, condition, and resources.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 20–21, 23–24
sections.body:
Health promotion means supporting and encouraging wellness. Nurses work at every level: individual, family, community, and population. The goal is to empower people to improve their quality of life.

National goals are led by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) and guided by the Office of Disease Prevention and Health Promotion (ODPHP). Programs include Healthy People 2030 and the President’s Council on Sports, Fitness and Nutrition. They set national goals and leading health indicators. They focus on reducing disparities, improving quality of life, and tracking population health.

A population goal is not a personal prescription. Strategies must fit the person’s age and condition. Consider developmental stage, health literacy, access to care, support systems, cultural beliefs, and past health care experiences.

rows: Assess age, literacy, prenatal care access, and support. Address conditions like gestational diabetes and high BP. Discuss birth setting and vaccine concerns.
Promote activity and limit screen time to under 2 hours a day. Prevent obesity. Encourage healthy snacks and family meal planning.
Encourage daily activity and independence. Assess fall risk and home safety. Support social ties and caregivers. Increase preventive screening (HTN, cancer, diabetes).

sections.heading: What risk factors and habits should I assess?
sections.keyIdea: Find the modifiable risks and coach the healthy habits the course lists; modifiable means changeable, not easy.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 25–26
sections.body:
Chronic disease is widespread and costly. Six in 10 U.S. adults have a chronic illness, and 4 in 10 have two or more (CDC, 2020). Chronic conditions make up 90% of the $3.5 trillion spent on health care each year.

Nurses identify risk factors. Nonmodifiable risks cannot change. Modifiable risks can. The focus is on preventable behaviors. But modifiable does not mean easy. Work hours, disability, food access, stress, and culture all shape choices.
bullets: Regular physical activity: 150 minutes a week (about 30 minutes a day).
Balanced diet: fruits, vegetables, whole grains, low sugar and fat.
Avoid tobacco and limit alcohol.
Sleep 7–9 hours a night.
Manage stress with mindfulness, laughter, or relaxation.
Stay up to date with screenings and immunizations.

sections.heading: How do beliefs and thoughts shape choices?
sections.keyIdea: Health beliefs, locus of control, and self-concept affect motivation, so explore them before teaching.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 27–28; self-efficacy added for the NCLEX
sections.body:
Health beliefs are what a person believes about illness, treatment, and wellness. They come from personal experience, culture, and family values.

Locus of control is internal when a person believes they can influence their health. It is external when they believe outside factors control it. Self-concept is how people see themselves: self-esteem, body image, roles, and abilities. These beliefs affect motivation, coping, and treatment decisions.

Thoughts lead to feelings, feelings to behaviors, and behaviors to outcomes. Negative thinking can trigger stress, anxiety, illness, and burnout. Positive reframing improves mood and coping. Nurses help clients notice and reframe distorted thinking. Stress management is essential.

Self-efficacy, a common NCLEX term, is confidence in doing one specific thing. Small successes build it.
bullets: “My father had a heart attack, so it doesn’t matter what I do.” Explore the belief. Then explain that inherited and lifestyle risks both count.
“My health is in God’s hands.” Ask what that belief means for their care before building a plan.
“I never stick with anything.” Choose one tiny, doable step to build confidence.

sections.heading: What are the stages of change?
sections.keyIdea: Use the client’s words to find their stage of change, then match your next step to that stage. Relapse is common and expected.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 29
sections.body:
Changing behavior is hard. Willpower alone is not enough. The Transtheoretical Model says motivation builds through six stages.

Change is not linear. Relapse is common and expected. It is a reason to find triggers and revise the plan, not proof that change is impossible.

Do not hand a detailed quit plan to someone not yet considering change. Do not lecture about risks to someone who already has a plan. They need resources and follow-up.

rows: “I don’t see a reason to stop.”
Explore beliefs. Offer information with permission.
“Part of me wants to, but I’m afraid.”
Explore the mixed feelings and confidence.
“I picked a quit date and downloaded an app.”
Help with concrete first steps and resources.
“I quit 3 weeks ago; evenings are hard.”
Troubleshoot triggers, affirm effort, arrange support.
Reinforce strategies and plan for setbacks.
“I don’t even think about smoking now.”
Termination: change fully part of life (rarely reached)
Affirm the change. Keep routine follow-up.

sections.heading: How do I talk to build motivation?
sections.keyIdea: Empathy, affirmations, open-ended questions, and reflection build motivation; blame, threats, and lectures shut it down.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 36
sections.body:
Implementation puts the plan into action. It requires therapeutic communication. Focus on motivation, readiness, and partnership, not just education.

Empathy means understanding feelings and reducing stress. Do not claim to know exactly how they feel. Affirmations encourage confidence and self-worth, like “You found a way to eat vegetables even on double-shift days.” Open-ended questions explore thoughts and feelings. Reflection repeats and validates what the client shares, so they can correct you.

Let the client choose the first change. Ask which change feels most possible. Remember: you can support an adult’s choices, but you cannot control them.

rows: “You want to cut back but drinking is how you unwind.”
“If you keep drinking, you’ll ruin your liver.”
“If you do this, you will never get sick.”

sections.heading: How do I write a SMART-EST goal?
sections.keyIdea: A strong goal names what the client will do, how much, how often, and when you will review it.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 32–35, 37
sections.body:
Use the nursing process, called ADPIE. Assess habits, beliefs, readiness, resources, and support. Diagnose problems, risks, and wellness strengths. Plan with the client and the interprofessional team. Implement. Evaluate and revise.

SMART means specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound. The course adds EST: evidence-based, strategic, and tailored.

“Exercise more” has no clear endpoint, so it cannot be measured. A better goal is: “For the next week, I will walk indoors for five minutes after breakfast on four days, as tolerated, and record symptoms.”

Fit the start point to the client. Set a review date.
steps: Ask the client to choose the behavior and say why it matters.
Assess ability, safety, readiness, and access.
Agree on an action, amount, frequency, and review date.
Plan support and a response to likely barriers.
Compare results with the goal and revise together.

sections.heading: What about integrative care and social support?
sections.keyIdea: Complementary care blends with conventional care, alternative care replaces it, and social support makes change last.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 30–31; supplement safety added for the NCLEX
sections.body:
U.S. health care has focused on “sick care.” Rising costs and client demand are shifting it toward wellness and prevention.

Alternative care replaces conventional medicine. It is rare, such as special diets instead of chemotherapy. Complementary care blends nontraditional and conventional treatments, such as yoga, massage, acupuncture, or supplements. Integrative health care combines evidence-based medicine and wellness practices. It focuses on mind, body, and spirit through partnership.

Ask about every product without judgment. “Natural” does not mean safe. A client on warfarin who starts ginkgo needs pharmacist or prescriber review. If a client replaced a prescribed drug, check their status and coordinate with the provider.

Supportive environments make change last. Isolation is a major health risk, comparable to smoking and obesity. Nurses foster connection.
bullets: Groups at risk for isolation: older adults, low-income families, immigrants, LGBTQ+ individuals, and people with chronic illness.
COVID-19 isolation increased depression, anxiety, and stress.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Most traps confuse the action with its purpose, or the nurse’s timeline with the client’s readiness.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 22, 29, 31; other rows added for the NCLEX
sections.body: Use this table to separate ideas that look alike on exam questions.

rows: Teaching can be any level. Ask if the condition already exists.
High risk with no problem yet is still primary.
Screening detects disease early. That is secondary.
Planning steps is preparation. Doing the behavior is action.
Relapse is common and expected. Explore triggers and revise.
Complementary adds to care. Alternative replaces it, which raises safety concerns.
Targets guide populations. Start each client at their baseline.
Brochures handed out is activity. People getting care is outcome.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Identify the stage or prevention level from the stem, then choose the response that fits it.
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials
sections.body:
Expect “which level of prevention” items, select-all lists, and stage-of-change statements. You may also see goal-writing items and follow-up after a relapse.

Sample question: A client says, “My grandfather smoked until he was 90. I don’t see any reason to quit.” Which response is best?
steps: Read the stem: the client sees no reason to change.
What is it really asking? Which stage is this, and what fits that stage?
Key cues: “I don’t see any reason” shows precontemplation.
Wrong options: Choosing a quit date skips ahead to preparation. Warning about lung disease is a threat. Saying the grandfather was lucky argues with the client.
The answer: An open question, such as “What do you enjoy about smoking, and has anything about it ever worried you?” It explores beliefs first.
Strategy: Name the stage from the client’s words, then pick the matching action.

sections.heading: Worked case: readiness changes the next step
sections.keyIdea: Mixed feelings mean contemplation, so explore them before you offer a quit plan.
sections.source: Added: worked example based on Module 7 slides 29, 36
sections.body:
Mr. J says he is thinking about quitting tobacco. He worries it is his only way to cope with stressful shifts. He has not set a date.

A detailed quit calendar now gives good information at the wrong time. He is in contemplation. Explore what he likes and dislikes about smoking and what else helps with stress.

Reflect without approving the risk: “You want the health benefit, but you worry about losing a way to cope.” Later, if he picks a date and gathers help, he is in preparation. If he relapses after starting, explore the trigger. Do not treat the relapse as proof he was not serious.
steps: Use his words to find his stage: contemplation.
Explore mixed feelings before assuming commitment.
Ask what support he would find useful.
Build concrete steps once he is preparing.
After a relapse, review triggers and revise the plan.

check.q: What would show Mr. J moving from contemplation to preparation?
check.a: A specific plan with practical steps, such as choosing a quit date and arranging support. Knowing the risks alone is not preparation.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.source: Module 7 slides 20–37 (course notes and clarifications)
sections.body: Use these notes to connect the lesson with your course materials.
bullets: Source: Module 7, slides 20–37.
Prevention levels, national goals, risk factors, beliefs, stages of change, communication skills, integrative care, and SMART-EST come from the course slides.
Self-efficacy, supplement safety, and the examples are added to help you apply the slides.
The course uses “relapse” for slipping back during change. Some texts call a brief slip a “lapse.”

mnemonics.name: Prevent, Screen, Support
mnemonics.text: Primary = Prevent it before it occurs. Secondary = Screen to detect and treat it early. Tertiary = Support recovery and reduce its impact.

mnemonics.name: Please Come Prepared And Motivated Today

pearls: Education can be primary, secondary, or tertiary. Classify by purpose.
Screening people with no known diagnosis is secondary prevention.
Use the client’s stated readiness, not your enthusiasm, to choose the next step.
A measurable behavior beats “understands healthy living.”
Low confidence improves with small successes, not more information.
Evaluate programs by whether people got care or changed behavior.
redFlags: New exertional symptoms, like chest pain with activity, need evaluation before any exercise plan.
A client who replaced a prescribed drug with an unreviewed product needs assessment and coordination now.
Supplements can interact with drugs like warfarin. Coordinate pharmacist or prescriber review.

checks.q: A client with COPD learns energy conservation. Which level of prevention is this?
checks.a: Tertiary. The disease already exists, and the goal is to reduce its impact and support function.

checks.q: A client has chosen a quit date but has not stopped smoking. Which stage fits?
checks.a: Preparation. Planning and gathering resources come before action.

checks.q: What is wrong with the goal “the client will understand exercise”?
checks.a: It cannot be observed. State what the client will do or show, how much, and when you will check.

checks.q: A client who quit smoking two months ago smoked three cigarettes at a party. What should the nurse do?
checks.a: Recognize the progress, explore the trigger, and revise the plan together. Relapse is common and expected, not failure.

checks.q: A nursing student says a client recovering from pneumonia “needs 150 minutes of activity this week.” What is the problem?
checks.a: That is a population target. Start from the client’s assessed baseline and progress gradually.

topics.title: Physical Fitness, Exercise & Safe Activity
topics.summary: Learn the types and benefits of exercise, then fit activity to the client’s ability, goals, symptoms, and surroundings, and know when to stop.
objectives: You can tell physical activity, exercise, and fitness apart.
You can match aerobic, anaerobic, endurance, strength, interval, and flexibility work to a goal.
You can name isotonic, isometric, and isokinetic exercise from what the joint does.
You can use the talk test and lifespan guidelines safely.
You can name the stop-and-report symptoms during activity.
You can plan, delegate, and evaluate activity care.
topics.bigPicture:
Physical activity is any movement that uses muscles and energy. Exercise is planned, repeated activity done to improve fitness. Walking to the bus is activity. A planned walking routine to build stamina is exercise.

Nursing care starts with what the client can safely do today. The goal is better function and real participation in life. People who use wheelchairs, have chronic disease, or are deconditioned can still exercise. Their plan is simply adapted. Progress is measured against their own starting point, with close attention to symptoms.
recap: Activity is any energy-using movement. Exercise is planned activity to build fitness.
Isometric: muscle tightens, joint does not move. Isotonic: the joint moves.
Isokinetic means controlled movement at a constant speed using equipment, often in rehab.
Talk test: moderate means you can talk but not sing. Vigorous means only a few words.
Adults: 150–300 moderate or 75–150 vigorous minutes weekly, plus strength work on 2 or more days.
Children and teens: at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity every day.
Stop and assess for chest discomfort, severe new breathlessness, dizziness, or near-fainting.
Guidelines are targets, not starting doses. Start from the client’s baseline.

keyTerms.def: Any movement using skeletal muscles that increases energy use.
Planned, purposeful, repeated activity to improve fitness.
Well-being in the physical dimension of wellness, from exercise, nutrition, sleep, and avoiding harmful substances.
Exercise that uses oxygen for energy, like swimming or cycling. It builds stamina.
Exercise that uses stored glucose without oxygen, like sprinting or heavy lifting. It builds strength and power.
The muscle contracts with movement against resistance, like a squat or biceps curl.
Muscle tension without joint movement, like a plank or quadriceps set.
Controlled movement at a constant speed using equipment. Often used in rehab.
Holding the breath while straining. It can spike blood pressure during isometric effort.
A simple way to judge exercise intensity by how easily a person can talk.
The ability to finish an activity with a safe body response and manageable symptoms.
Loss of strength and stamina from illness or inactivity.
Feeling about to faint, often with dizziness or vision changes.

sections.heading: What are fitness, activity, and exercise?
sections.keyIdea: Activity is any muscle movement that uses energy; exercise is planned activity to build fitness. Both help every body system and the mind.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 40–42, 46–47
sections.body:
Physical fitness is well-being in the physical dimension of wellness. It comes from regular exercise, balanced nutrition, enough sleep and rest, and avoiding harmful substances. It raises endurance, strength, mobility, balance, coordination, and agility. It lowers the risk of chronic disease, disability, and illness.

Physical activity is any movement using skeletal muscles that increases energy use. Walking, gardening, and ADLs count. “Move more, sit less.” Every minute counts.

Exercise is planned, purposeful, repeated activity to improve fitness. It is preventive, curative, and restorative. Choose activities the client enjoys and can keep doing.

Ask which benefit matters most. A client may care more about gardening again than about a future risk. Do not promise exercise will prevent every disease.

rows: ↑ heart strength, circulation, HDL. ↓ BP, inflammation, heart disease risk.
↑ lung capacity and oxygen efficiency. ↓ dyspnea in COPD and asthma.
↑ muscle mass, bone density, joint stability, flexibility. ↓ fall risk.
Better metabolism and gut health. ↓ colon cancer, IBD, obesity risk.
↑ insulin sensitivity and glucose control. ↓ type 2 diabetes risk.
Stronger immunity. ↓ risk of several cancers.
Better memory, focus, sleep, and mood. ↓ anxiety, depression, dementia, Parkinson disease risk. Builds new brain connections (neuroplasticity).

sections.heading: What types of exercise are there?
sections.keyIdea: Aerobic exercise uses oxygen and builds stamina; anaerobic uses stored glucose without oxygen and builds strength and power. Combining both improves fitness.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 43–44
sections.body:
Aerobic exercise uses oxygen for energy. Examples are swimming, running, dancing, and cycling. It builds stamina and heart and lung endurance.

Anaerobic exercise uses stored glucose without oxygen. Examples are sprinting, heavy lifting, and HIIT. It builds muscle strength and power. Combining both improves overall fitness.

The course also sorts exercise into four training categories. A full plan often mixes several. Match the activity to the client’s goal and what they can do now. Interval training is not automatically right for a beginner or someone medically unstable.

rows: Improves balance and range of motion

sections.heading: Isotonic, isometric, or isokinetic?
sections.keyIdea: Name the type by what the joint does: moves against resistance, stays still, or moves at a constant speed set by equipment.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 45; breath-holding caution added for the NCLEX
sections.body:
Isotonic exercise is a muscle contracting with movement against resistance. Examples are squats, stair climbing, and biceps curls. It builds bone density, strength, and joint mobility.

Isometric exercise is muscle tension without joint movement. Examples are planks, wall sits, yoga poses, and quadriceps sets. It improves stability and can be adapted for limited mobility, such as a leg in a cast.

Isokinetic exercise is controlled movement at a constant speed using equipment. Course examples are adaptive resistance machines, stationary bikes, and treadmills. It is often used in rehab to rebuild strength safely.

Isometric effort can raise blood pressure sharply if the client holds their breath. Teach clients to keep breathing. Use caution with heart disease.
sections.analogy: Isotonic: lift and lower a grocery bag. Isometric: push against a wall that will not move. Isokinetic: a rehab machine sets the speed for you.
sections.example: A client in a long leg cast wants to keep thigh strength. Teach quadriceps sets, which are isometric. Remind the client to breathe normally during each hold.

sections.heading: How hard is the client working?
sections.keyIdea: Moderate means the client can talk but not sing; vigorous means only a few words before pausing for breath.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 44; beta-blocker and safety tips added for the NCLEX
sections.body:
The talk test is a quick way to judge intensity. It works for stable clients. It does not replace assessment or rehab orders.

The course safety rule is “Challenge yourself, not your limits.” Avoid pain to prevent injury.

Some drugs change the body’s response. Beta blockers, such as metoprolol, keep the heart rate low. A client on one may never reach a heart rate target. Guide intensity by the talk test and symptoms instead.

The talk test shows intensity. It does not show the total amount of activity for the week.

rows: Can talk but cannot sing comfortably
Can say only a few words before pausing for breath

bullets: Teach a warm-up first.
Use safe footwear and proper equipment.
Progress slowly from the starting point.
Keep breathing normally. Do not hold the breath.
Know which symptoms mean stop and who to call.

sections.heading: How much activity is recommended?
sections.keyIdea: Guidelines are targets for each age group, so start each client where they are and build up.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 26, 48
sections.body:
Children and teens (6–17 years) need at least 60 minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous activity. Include aerobic, muscle-strengthening, and bone-strengthening activity. Gym class twice a week is not enough.

Adults (18–64) aim for 150–300 minutes a week of moderate activity, or 75–150 minutes of vigorous activity. Add muscle strengthening on 2 or more days. These are weekly totals.

Older adults (65+) follow the adult guidelines as able and add balance training to prevent falls. Pregnant and postpartum people aim for at least 150 minutes a week of moderate activity. They avoid high-risk or supine (flat on the back) positions after the first trimester. People with chronic conditions or disabilities should be as active as their abilities allow, under health care provider guidance.

rows: Start with short, doable bouts. Build up slowly.
Add balance training with safety support.
Be as active as able, under provider guidance.
No high-risk or supine positions after the first trimester. Coordinate with the obstetric team.

sections.example: A sedentary adult says, “I need 150 minutes, so I’ll walk 150 minutes on Saturday.” Explain that 150 is a weekly total. Start with shorter walks and build up.

sections.heading: How do I assess and support activity?
sections.keyIdea: Check safety, ability, confidence, and access, then use the course’s nursing interventions to support activity.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 49; assessment points added for the NCLEX
sections.body:
Ask about usual activity, symptoms, falls, pain, devices, and what the client enjoys. Review diagnoses, restrictions, and medicines.

Ability and confidence differ. A client may be strong enough to walk but afraid of falling. Another may be willing but have no safe place to walk. “Join a gym” fails if the client cannot afford it.

Assess readiness, too. Refer to physical or occupational therapy for rehab and equipment needs.
bullets: Model healthy exercise attitudes and behaviors.
Set SMART goals with the client and plan follow-up.
Teach stretching, warm-up, and self-care strategies.
Encourage family and community participation.
Teach safe use of exercise tools and equipment.
Advocate for access to gyms, parks, and safe spaces.
Support motivation, acknowledge barriers, and celebrate progress.

sections.heading: When must activity stop?
sections.keyIdea: New chest discomfort, severe breathlessness, dizziness, or near-fainting means stop now and assess.
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials (builds on the slide 44 safety rule)
sections.body:
Pain is not proof that exercise is working. Sharp pain during exercise means stop and assess.

If a client feels faint while walking, stop and get them safely seated first. Then assess.

Review unstable illness with the provider before starting or advancing exercise. A client with very high blood pressure should not start a high-intensity class tomorrow. In pregnancy, a warning sign means stop and get prompt obstetric evaluation.

The RN can delegate routine walks for stable clients to assistive personnel (UAP). The RN keeps assessment, teaching, evaluation, and decisions to progress. If a UAP reports chest symptoms after a walk, the RN assesses the client personally and promptly.
bullets: New chest discomfort or pressure
Severe or new shortness of breath
Dizziness or near-fainting
Sharp new pain

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Classify by mechanism and judge readiness by assessment, not by motivation or minutes.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 44–45, 48; other rows added for the NCLEX
sections.body: These pairs look alike on the exam. Here is how to tell them apart.

rows: Joint still is isometric. Joint moving against resistance is isotonic.
Isokinetic uses equipment to keep a constant speed. Isotonic is free movement against resistance, like squats.
Talk but not sing is moderate. Few words only is vigorous.
150 minutes is per week, not all at once or per day.
Adults also need strength work on 2 or more days.
Eagerness is not a safety check. Assess tolerance first.
Expected soreness differs from chest pain or near-fainting.
Track endurance, recovery, function, and confidence.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Safety symptoms beat targets, and the RN keeps assessment, teaching, and evaluation.
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials
sections.body:
Expect contraction-type items, talk-test items, and guideline numbers. Priority items ask which client in a walking program needs follow-up first. Delegation items ask which activity task fits a UAP.

Sample question: A stable client begins a planned walk and reports new chest pressure and marked shortness of breath. What should the nurse do first?
steps: Read the stem: a stable client, a planned walk, new chest pressure, and marked breathlessness.
What is it really asking? Does a red-flag symptom override the exercise plan?
Key cues: “New” and “marked” signal a change, not normal effort.
Wrong options: Lowering the intensity keeps the client exercising. Checking the pulse against a training range puts a number ahead of symptoms. Walking back to document first delays assessment.
The answer: Stop the activity, help the client rest safely, and assess right away.
Strategy: If a symptom suggests heart or breathing trouble, stop first and assess.

sections.heading: Worked case: function before a target
sections.keyIdea: A valued goal guides the plan, but assess tolerance and route safety before starting.
sections.source: Added: worked example based on Module 7 slides 44, 48–49
sections.body:
Mrs. B fell two months ago. She uses a cane indoors and tires quickly. She wants to walk to a nearby shop again. The route has uneven pavement.

A weekly activity target is background only. It does not prove she can do this route safely today. Ask what the shop visit means to her. It might be independence, friendship, or getting food.

A therapist can check her technique and device. Community services can help with access while she builds endurance. Teach her the stop signs. Moderate effort is expected. New chest pressure means stop and get help.
steps: Connect activity to her goal: walking to the shop.
Assess baseline walking, symptoms, falls, device, and the route.
Pick a safe start, such as short indoor walks with rests.
Teach stop-and-report symptoms.
Evaluate with details, like “walked 5 minutes with one rest, no symptoms.”

check.q: Why does meeting a weekly minute target not prove Mrs. B is ready for the shop route?
check.a: The route also needs balance on uneven ground, safe device use, and enough reserve for the trip. Minutes alone do not show those abilities.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.source: Module 7 slides 38–49 (course notes and clarifications)
sections.body: Use these notes to connect the lesson with your course materials.
bullets: Source: Module 7, Exemplar 7.A, slides 38–49.
Isokinetic exercise: controlled movement at a constant speed using equipment. The slide’s examples are adaptive resistance machines, stationary bikes, and treadmills. Use these for course exams.
Clinical note: true isokinetic rehab devices hold the speed constant whatever force the client uses.
Aerobic and anaerobic follow the slide: oxygen for energy vs. stored glucose without oxygen. In real life most activities use both.
Stop signs, delegation, and beta-blocker tips are added for the NCLEX. Activity targets still require individual assessment.

mnemonics.name: Three “iso” words
mnemonics.text: Isometric = muscle tight, joint motionless. Isotonic = joint moves against resistance (think “toning” with curls). Isokinetic = kept at constant speed by equipment.

pearls: Classify a contraction by what the joint does: moves, stays still, or moves at a constant set speed.
Moderate intensity: the client can talk but not sing.
With a beta blocker, guide intensity by the talk test and symptoms.
Individualize guideline totals to current capacity.
Document distance, assistance, symptoms, and recovery, not “tolerated well.”
Delegate routine walks for stable clients. Keep assessment, teaching, and evaluation.
redFlags: Stop activity and assess for new chest discomfort, severe breathlessness, dizziness, or near-fainting.
If a client feels faint while walking, get them safely seated first, then assess.
Review unstable illness, new injury, or restrictions before starting or advancing activity.
A warning sign during pregnancy means stop and get prompt obstetric evaluation.

checks.q: A client tightens the thigh muscle while the knee stays still. What type of contraction is this?
checks.a: Isometric. The muscle develops tension without joint movement.

checks.q: A rehab client uses an adaptive resistance machine that keeps the movement at a constant speed. What type of exercise is this?
checks.a: Isokinetic. It is controlled movement at a constant speed using equipment, often used in rehab.

checks.q: A runner can say only a few words before taking a breath. What intensity is this, and how many minutes a week meet the aerobic minimum?
checks.a: Vigorous. Seventy-five vigorous minutes a week meets the adult aerobic minimum.

checks.q: A parent says her 9-year-old has gym twice a week, so she gets enough exercise. How should the nurse respond?
checks.a: Explain that school-age children need at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity every day.

checks.q: What should the nurse assess before recommending daily outdoor walking?
checks.a: Baseline ability, symptoms, fall risk, devices, restrictions, preferences, and a safe, accessible route.

topics.title: Oral Health, Assessment & Daily Care
topics.summary: Oral care supports comfort, eating, speech, and dignity. Assess the mouth, the client’s ability to do care, swallowing safety, and access to dental services.
objectives: You can describe the main mouth structures and what saliva does.
You can tell plaque, tartar, cavities, gingivitis, and periodontal disease apart.
You can assess oral habits, function, risk, and access to dental care.
You can teach both the course and current fluoride and dental-visit guidance for children.
You can give safe oral care to clients with aspiration risk or dentures.
You can decide what to delegate and how to evaluate oral care.
topics.bigPicture:
A sore or dry mouth makes it hard to eat, talk, swallow, and socialize. A client who cannot grip a toothbrush, or cannot remember the steps, may lose oral health even after teaching. Oral care is a nursing assessment and comfort issue. It is not just about looks.

Look beyond the teeth. Check lips, gums, tongue, the inside lining of the mouth, saliva, dentures, pain, and how much the client can do. Nurses keep the mouth clean and comfortable. They also arrange dental care for disease, lasting sores, or tooth pain.
recap: Oral health supports eating, speaking, comfort, and dignity.
Plaque is a soft film. Tartar is hardened plaque that needs professional removal.
Early decay can be reversed with fluoride and minerals. An established cavity needs a dentist.
Bleeding gums need gentle, continued brushing and assessment, never stopping care.
Slide: brush with water at 18 months. Current guidance: rice-sized fluoride smear from the first tooth.
Slide: first dental visit by 6 months. Current guidance: dental home by the first birthday.
Aspiration risk changes how oral care is done, not whether it is done.
Facial swelling with fever, drooling, or trouble swallowing is an airway emergency.

keyTerms.def: Chewing. It is the mechanical start of digestion.
The moist pink lining inside the mouth and cheeks.
The hard outer covering of the visible tooth crown.
The soft inner part of a tooth that holds nerves and blood vessels.
An enzyme in saliva that starts breaking down starches.
A soft, sticky film of bacteria on the teeth.
Hardened plaque that irritates gums and damages bone. A dental professional must remove it.
Tooth decay. Bacteria turn sugars and starches into acid that breaks down enamel.
Gum inflammation, often with redness, swelling, and bleeding.
Disease of the deeper tissues that hold teeth in place. It can cause gum recession and loose teeth.
The course term for advanced periodontal disease, with pus, receding gums, and loose teeth.
Dry mouth, often from less saliva due to medicines or illness.
An ongoing relationship with one dental office for regular care.
Fluid, food, or secretions entering the airway and lungs.
Difficulty swallowing.
Unlicensed assistive personnel, such as nursing assistants. The RN delegates routine tasks for stable clients to them.

sections.heading: Why does the mouth matter?
sections.keyIdea: Oral health is more than teeth. It supports eating and speech and is linked to heart disease, pneumonia, diabetes, and more.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 52–53
sections.body:
Oral health goes beyond healthy teeth. It includes the mouth, gums, tongue, mucosa, and jaw. It supports speaking, chewing, tasting, swallowing, smiling, and communication.

Oral health is linked to heart disease, stroke, pneumonia, pregnancy outcomes, diabetes, and dementia. Prevention works: daily hygiene, fluoridated water, dental sealants, tobacco cessation, and regular exams. Disparities persist. One in 4 preschoolers has decay. One in 4 adults over 65 has lost all their teeth.

A dry or painful mouth can quietly reduce eating. A client may skip meals because chewing hurts. Address the mouth, not just the intake numbers.
bullets: Structures: lips, cheeks, teeth, gums, tongue, hard and soft palates, salivary glands, uvula, and tonsils.
Tooth parts: the crown is the visible part, covered with enamel. The pulp cavity holds blood vessels and nerves. The root anchors the tooth in the jawbone.
Mastication (chewing) is the first step in digestion.
Saliva moistens food and starts starch breakdown with the enzyme amylase.
The soft palate and uvula direct food into the esophagus during swallowing.
Development: 20 deciduous (baby) teeth by age 2. Permanent teeth replace them by about age 6–7. Enamel wears with age, which raises decay risk.

sections.heading: Plaque, tartar, cavities, or gum disease?
sections.keyIdea: Soft plaque responds to daily care, hard tartar needs a dentist, and gingivitis can progress to pyorrhea.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 54
sections.body:
Dental caries (cavities) happen when bacteria turn sugars and starches into acid. The acid breaks down enamel. This causes decay and permanent damage. Early decay can be reversed with fluoride and minerals, such as calcium. An established cavity does not heal with brushing. It needs dental repair.

Plaque is a soft, sticky bacterial film on teeth. Tartar is hardened plaque. It irritates gums and damages bone, and it needs professional cleaning.

Periodontal disease begins as gingivitis: red, swollen, bleeding gums. It can progress to pyorrhea: pus, receding gums, and loose teeth. It is linked to poor hygiene, diet, and chronic illness.

Bleeding gums are a cue to assess technique and refer. They are not a reason to stop brushing.

rows: Arrange dental cleaning. Keep up daily care.
Gentle brushing, assess, and refer as needed.

sections.heading: What should the oral assessment include?
sections.keyIdea: Ask about habits and symptoms, inspect the mouth, and know which clients are at higher risk.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 57–58
sections.body:
Use observation and interview. Inspect for lesions, bleeding, odor, dryness, pain, and loose teeth. Record exact sites and findings, not “mouth bad.” Compare with earlier findings.

Check function. Can the client grip a brush, see the supplies, follow steps, and handle secretions? Weak hands, memory loss, and pain each need a different fix.

Medicines such as diuretics, antihistamines, and anticonvulsants can cause xerostomia (dry mouth) or gingival hyperplasia (overgrown gums). Report concerns to the prescriber. Never stop a prescribed drug on your own.
bullets: Ask adults: daily oral care routine and products, dental visits and pain history, bleeding, swelling, dryness, or ulcers, and tobacco use or exposure.
Ask about children: diet, fluoride intake, bottle use, bedtime habits, and smoke exposure.
At risk: chronic illness such as diabetes, HIV/AIDS, or autoimmune disorders.
At risk: poor nutrition or hydration.
At risk: after oral surgery or radiation therapy.
At risk: medicine side effects (diuretics, antihistamines, anticonvulsants).
At risk: limited access to dental care or low income.
sections.example: A resident with advanced dementia cannot describe pain. She has refused meals for 3 days and guards her jaw. Inspect her mouth first. Pain there may be the cause.

sections.heading: How do I protect teeth from infancy to adulthood?
sections.keyIdea: Clean from the first tooth, avoid bottles in bed, and supervise brushing. Know the course timeline and the current fluoride update.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 55; current AAPD guidance added
sections.body:
Infants and toddlers. Begin cleaning when the first tooth erupts, at about 5–8 months. Wipe with moist gauze or a washcloth after feedings. Do not bottle-feed during sleep. This prevents “bottle mouth” decay.

Preschool and school-age. Brush after meals or twice daily. Limit sugary foods. Fluoride is important. Parents should supervise brushing. Keep baby teeth healthy to prevent misalignment.

Teens and adults. Reinforce a balanced diet and regular brushing and flossing. Discuss quitting tobacco. Tobacco is a major cause of gum disease, decay, and oral cancer. Encourage routine dental visits.
sections.example: A parent of an 18-month-old asks how to brush. Know the slide answer (water, then add fluoride gradually). In practice, teach caregiver brushing with a rice-sized smear of fluoride toothpaste, and ask whether the child has a dentist.

rows: Brush with water at 18 months; add fluoride toothpaste gradually
Fluoride toothpaste from the first tooth: rice-sized smear under age 3, pea-sized ages 3–6
By 6 months, for fluoride varnish education
Dental home at the first tooth, no later than the first birthday

sections.heading: What changes in pregnancy and older age?
sections.keyIdea: Pregnancy raises gum and enamel risks, and older adults risk dry mouth and tooth loss. Neither is a reason to skip dental care.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 56, 58
sections.body:
Pregnancy. Hormone changes raise the risk of gingivitis and bleeding gums. Nausea and vomiting expose teeth to acid and erode enamel. Routine dental care is safe during pregnancy. Teach a soft-bristled brush, rinsing after reflux or vomiting, and more water. Fluoride varnish may be recommended.

Older adults. Risks are xerostomia, gum disease, decay, and tooth loss. Causes include medicines, chronic illness, poor dexterity, and dementia. Encourage frequent sips of water and rinsing after meals. Use adaptive or electric brushes, or suction devices, as needed.

In long-term care, 80% of residents lack daily oral care. Nurses must assess, assist, and advocate. With a fluid restriction, keep moisture care within the fluid plan.
bullets: Dentures: clean daily with denture cleaner or mild toothpaste.
Store dentures safely, and offer privacy during removal.
A red, sore spot under a denture needs inspection and a fit check.
Moisture: saliva substitutes for xerostomia, and sips of water through the day if swallowing is safe.

sections.heading: How do I give oral care safely?
sections.keyIdea: Assist or perform oral care for dependent clients; if they cannot protect the airway, position side-lying, use little fluid, and suction.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 58; airway positioning added for the NCLEX
sections.body:
Daily hygiene means brushing and flossing, stimulating the gums, and rinsing the mouth. Assist or perform care for dependent or unconscious clients. Explain the care and let the client help as able.

Use a soft toothbrush or saline-soaked gauze if the mucosa is fragile. Provide special oral care every 2–8 hours as needed. Follow the care plan for how often.

Clients with low alertness, swallowing problems, or poor secretion control are at risk of aspiration. Position them as allowed, often side-lying with the head turned, so fluid drains out of the mouth. Use suction as needed. Never pour fluid into the mouth. Clients who are NPO (nothing by mouth) or tube-fed still need oral care.
steps: Assess alertness, swallowing, mouth findings, pain, and cooperation.
Explain the care and position the client safely.
Clean gently while controlling fluid and secretions with suction.
Inspect dentures and tissues, and add safe moisture.
Record findings, help given, tolerance, and follow-up.
sections.example: Right after oral care, a client with low alertness starts gurgling and the oxygen level drops. Clear the airway first. Call for help and document after.

sections.heading: Who does oral care, and did it work?
sections.keyIdea: Delegate routine care for stable clients, keep risky care yourself, and judge success by the client’s change.
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials (builds on slide 56 “assess, assist, and advocate”)
sections.body:
The RN can delegate routine oral care for stable clients to unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP). The RN keeps care that needs assessment. That includes a new or unknown swallowing risk, airway risk, or a new finding.

If a UAP says, “His gums bled, so I stopped brushing,” teach that bleeding gums need gentle brushing and assessment, not no brushing. If a delegated task creates an immediate choking risk, stop it and protect the airway first.

Evaluate outcomes. Giving an adapted brush is an intervention. The outcome is the client using it, with less pain and healthier tissue. For a caregiver, watch a safe return demonstration.
bullets: Ask about comfort. Look for less debris and dryness.
Can the client eat or speak more easily?
Persistent sores, tooth pain, swelling, pus, unexplained bleeding, or loose teeth need evaluation.
Oral and body disease are linked, but do not claim one always causes the other.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Do not let a label, an old belief, or a delivered intervention replace assessment.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 54, 56–58; other rows added for the NCLEX
sections.body: These look-alike ideas often appear in wrong answer choices.

rows: Plaque is soft and brushes off. Tartar is hard and needs a dentist.
Early decay can be reversed with fluoride and minerals. A cavity needs restoration.
Red, bleeding gums are gingivitis. Pus, receding gums, and loose teeth are pyorrhea.
Dryness has causes. Assess medicines, fluids, and illness.
NPO changes how care is done, not whether it is needed.
Keep brushing gently. Assess and refer.
A painful mouth can be the real reason for eating less.
Outcome means the client uses it with better comfort.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Airway safety comes first, then comfort and function, then teaching and referral.
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials
sections.body:
Expect priority items about drowsy or unresponsive clients, select-all lists of urgent findings, and pediatric fluoride questions. Delegation items ask which client’s oral care fits a UAP.

Sample question: A drowsy client with poor secretion control needs oral care. Which action is the priority before cleaning begins?
steps: Read the stem: drowsy client, poor secretion control, oral care.
What is it really asking? What protects this client from aspiration?
Key cues: “Drowsy” and “poor secretion control” mean airway risk.

Wrong options: Choosing a product and cleaning first skips the airway. Cleaning dentures before checking rinse safety is out of order. Asking about home routines while setting up a standard rinse ignores the risk.
The answer: Assess airway safety and prepare side-lying positioning and suction.
Strategy: When swallowing or alertness is impaired, protect the airway before anything else.

sections.heading: Worked case: poor intake starts in the mouth
sections.keyIdea: When intake drops and the mouth hurts, treat the mouth problem as a possible cause.
sections.source: Added: worked example based on Module 7 slides 53, 56–58
sections.body:
An older adult eats little and says food tastes bad. Her mouth is dry. Her dentures hurt. Stiff hands make brushing hard.

Calling this a nutrition knowledge problem and handing over a food sheet misses the cause. Her appetite may be fine. Mouth pain may stop her from eating.

Check swallowing safety before offering water sips. If fluids are restricted, keep moisture care within the plan. Do not stop a medicine just because it may cause dryness. Report it instead.
steps: Assess mouth pain, denture fit, tissue, saliva, swallowing, medicines, and fluid limits.
Ask which problem started first and what happens when she eats.
Give gentle help, safe moisture, and an adapted brush.
Arrange a dental visit she can actually get to.
Reassess chewing, comfort, intake, and whether she can use the brush.

check.q: In this case, what is an intervention and what is an outcome?
check.a: Giving an adapted brush is an intervention. The client using it well, with better comfort and eating, is the outcome.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.source: Module 7 slides 50–58 (course notes and current guidance)
sections.body: Use these notes to connect the lesson with your course materials.
bullets: Source: Module 7, Exemplar 7.B, slides 50–58.
Course slide: brush with water at 18 months, add fluoride toothpaste gradually, and first dental visit by 6 months.
Current AAPD guidance: fluoride toothpaste from the first tooth (rice-sized smear under age 3; pea-sized ages 3–6), and a dental home no later than the first birthday. Checked October 27, 2026.
This is a stated clinical update, not a quote from the slide. Know the slide for course exams.
The slide’s 2–8 hour special-care range does not replace individual risk assessment.
Delegation and airway-priority points are added for the NCLEX.

pearls: Assess dry mouth for a cause instead of calling it normal aging.
Trouble swallowing changes the oral-care technique, not the need for it.
Prevention starts with the first tooth.
Brushing does not reverse an established cavity.
For a hands-on caregiver skill, evaluate with a return demonstration.
Chronic illness, oral surgery, radiation, and some medicines raise oral risk.
redFlags: Facial swelling with fever, drooling, voice change, or trouble swallowing or breathing needs urgent action.
Low alertness and poor secretion control raise aspiration risk during oral care.
Gurgling or a drop in oxygen after oral care means clear the airway first.
Lasting sores, loose teeth, or pus need dental evaluation.

checks.q: How do plaque and tartar differ?
checks.a: Plaque is a soft bacterial film that brushing removes. Tartar is hardened plaque that needs professional removal.

checks.q: What changes when a drowsy client needs oral care?
checks.a: Protect the airway: side-lying position with the head turned, very little fluid, and suction as needed.

checks.q: How much fluoride toothpaste is used for a child under age 3?
checks.a: The slide says brush with water at 18 months and add fluoride gradually. Current AAPD guidance: a rice-sized smear, brushed by the caregiver from the first tooth.

checks.q: A client with heart failure on a 1,500 mL fluid restriction has a very dry mouth. What helps?
checks.a: Frequent oral care and moisture support that stays within the fluid limit, such as saliva substitutes.

checks.q: An older adult cannot grip a toothbrush. Is more explanation enough?
checks.a: No. Assess function, provide an adapted brush or help, and check that the client can actually do the care.

topics.title: Normal Sleep, Circadian Rhythm & Nursing Care
topics.summary: Assess both how much and how well a client sleeps, know normal age changes, and target the real causes of poor rest safely.
objectives: You can explain how sleep supports thinking, healing, and mood.
You can describe circadian rhythm and the N1, N2, N3, and REM stages.
You can tell normal age-related sleep changes from warning signs.
You can assess sleep onset, waking, quality, and daytime function.
You can choose sleep interventions that keep required care safe.
You can recognize when sleepiness is a danger sign.
topics.bigPicture:
Sleep is an active body process, not just “switching off.” The brain cycles through stages while awareness of the room fades. Sleep restores the body, builds memory, steadies emotions, and supports daily function.

Pain, stress, medicines, illness, and hospital routines can all break up sleep. So ask two questions: “How much are you sleeping?” and “How rested do you feel during the day?” Eight hours in bed may include many awakenings. Your nursing response depends on the pattern, its causes, and what the client wants.
recap: Hours in bed do not equal hours asleep. Assess quality and daytime function.
Current staging has three NREM stages (N1, N2, N3) plus REM.
Deep N3 sleep comes mostly early in the night. REM gets longer toward morning.
Older adults sleep lighter and earlier, but they do not need much less sleep.
Find and treat the cause, like pain, noise, or nocturia, before asking for a sleeping pill.
Cluster nonurgent care, but never skip required monitoring to protect sleep.
A client who cannot be awakened is not “just sleeping.” Assess immediately.
Alcohol may help a person fall asleep but disrupts sleep later.

keyTerms.def: The body’s 24-hour clock. It regulates sleep, body temperature, and hormones.
A hormone that rises in darkness and signals that it is night.
A brainstem network that, with the brainstem, controls sleep and wakefulness.
Non-rapid-eye-movement sleep. It now has three stages: N1, N2, and N3.
Deep sleep with delta waves, when growth and repair occur. The slides split it into N3 and N4.
Rapid-eye-movement sleep. The brain is active, dreams are common, and muscles normally relax.
The total hours slept.
How rested a person feels after sleep.
Habits and surroundings that support regular, restful sleep.
A daily log of sleep times, awakenings, naps, substances, symptoms, and daytime function.
Waking at night to urinate.
Sleep broken up by many awakenings.
A medicine that causes drowsiness or sleep. It can slow breathing and cause confusion or falls.
