Unlicensed assistive personnel, such as nursing assistants. They can do routine tasks but not assessment.

sections.heading: Why does sleep matter so much?
sections.keyIdea: Sleep is a basic human need for health and healing; lost sleep harms attention, mood, and judgment and raises chronic disease risk.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 61, 64–65
sections.body:
Sleep is a basic human need, essential for health and healing. It restores mind and body. It improves daytime alertness, energy, and quality of life. Over 50 million Americans have sleep disorders.

Sleep restores balance in the brain and nervous system. It supports protein synthesis for tissue repair and healing. It boosts immune function and reduces inflammation. It improves mood, focus, memory, and creativity. It also helps with weight control and stress.

Sleep deprivation lowers concentration, memory, and alertness. It causes irritability and poor decision-making. A tired client may be too exhausted to learn.

Poor sleep can be a problem by itself. It can also be a clue to another problem, like pain or a medicine effect.
sections.example: A client keeps dozing during insulin teaching after a night of pain. Treat the pain, reschedule key teaching, and check learning later. Do not chart “uninterested.”
bullets: Obesity and type 2 diabetes
High blood pressure, stroke, and heart disease
Depression, anxiety, and impaired judgment

sections.heading: How does the body control sleep?
sections.keyIdea: The RAS and brainstem control sleep, melatonin rises in darkness, and cortisol rises in the morning. Bright days and dark nights help the body clock.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 62–63
sections.body:
Sleep is an altered state of consciousness with less awareness of and response to stimuli. The reticular activating system (RAS) and brainstem control it.

The circadian rhythm is the body’s 24-hour clock. It regulates sleep, body temperature, and hormones. When it is in sync, a person is awake when body temperature is highest and asleep when it is lowest.

Shift work, bright rooms at night, and frequent interruptions can throw the clock off. A hospital client who naps all day and is awake at night may have a disrupted rhythm. Restore bright days and dark nights.

rows: See note: GABA activity actually supports sleep

sections.heading: What are NREM and REM sleep?
sections.keyIdea: A 90–110 minute cycle alternates NREM (about 80%) and REM (about 20%). Deep sleep does growth and repair; REM brings dreams.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 63; current three-stage NREM system added
sections.body:
A sleep cycle lasts about 90–110 minutes. It alternates between NREM (about 80% of sleep) and REM (about 20%).

In NREM, N1 and N2 are light sleep. The person wakes easily. Deep sleep has slow delta waves. Growth and repair happen there. Deep sleep is most common early in the night.

REM begins about 70–90 minutes after falling asleep. Dreams occur. Muscles relax. Heart rate and blood pressure rise. The brain is active. REM periods grow longer toward morning.

The slides label deep sleep as N3 and N4. Today these are combined into one stage, N3. So there are three NREM stages. A client who is suddenly hard to wake is not just in deep sleep. Assess right away.

rows: Easily awakened. Interruptions break up sleep.
Growth and repair. Less of it with age.
Dreams, relaxed muscles, ↑ HR and BP, active brain
Starts 70–90 minutes in. Longer toward morning.

sections.heading: How does sleep change with age?
sections.keyIdea: Know the course’s hours for each age group, but judge each client by total sleep and daytime function.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 65–66
sections.body:
Compare the client’s reported sleep with the recommended hours. Adults should average 7–9 hours a night.

Older adults go to bed and wake earlier. Their sleep is more fragmented. That does not mean they need almost no sleep. Watch for insomnia, nocturia, and sundowning in dementia.

Disabling daytime sleepiness, breathing pauses, or a big new change is not normal aging. It needs evaluation.

rows: Sleeps through the night by 6 months
Needs 2 naps a day. Babies vary.
Natural delay in sleep onset causes sleep loss.
Early bedtime and waking. Fragmented sleep.

sections.heading: How do I assess a sleep problem?
sections.keyIdea: Sort the problem (falling asleep vs. staying asleep), then check habits, environment, health, and substances.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 67–68
sections.body:
Sleep quantity is the total hours slept. Sleep quality is how rested you feel. Habits, environment, and health affect both.

First, sort the problem. Is it trouble falling asleep or staying asleep? Ask about bedtime, wake time, naps, work, and the bedroom. A sleep diary helps find patterns.

Compare with the home routine. A night-shift worker awake at 0200 may be on a normal schedule, not “noncompliant.” Snoring, witnessed breathing pauses, and daytime sleepiness need evaluation.
bullets: Exercise: moderate daytime activity helps sleep. Late exercise delays it.
Schedule: a regular bedtime and wake time support the body clock.
Bedtime habits: avoid work, screens, or caffeine before bed.
Stress and illness: anxiety and pain reduce deep and REM sleep.
Substances: caffeine, nicotine, alcohol, and some medicines disrupt sleep. Alcohol may cause drowsiness at first but breaks up sleep later. Never suggest it as a sleep aid.
Environment: a cool, dark, quiet room improves sleep.

sections.heading: What helps clients sleep?
sections.keyIdea: Target the cause, teach sleep hygiene, and reduce nighttime disruptions, but never skip required monitoring.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 68; clustering-care point added for the NCLEX
sections.body:
Fix what is breaking sleep. Treat pain. Help with position and temperature. For nocturia, keep nighttime toileting safe with a clear path and a call light within reach.

Advocate for quiet, restful health care settings. Group nonurgent care together when the plan allows. Essential checks, medicines, and tests still happen. Do them quietly.

Evaluate outcomes, not actions. “Room darkened” is an intervention. Fewer awakenings and better alertness are outcomes.

Keep familiar, safe bedtime rituals, such as prayer or music. For shift workers, teach a dark room, a regular sleep period, and no caffeine or alcohol before sleep.
bullets: Encourage a regular bedtime routine and a consistent schedule.
Reduce nighttime disruptions and noise.
Suggest a sleep diary to find patterns.
Promote relaxation, such as music, deep breathing, or mindfulness.
Teach healthy sleep hygiene.

sections.heading: When is sleepiness a danger sign?
sections.keyIdea: New confusion, hard-to-wake clients, and slowed breathing are emergencies, not sleep problems.
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials
sections.body:
A sleeping pill is not the first answer to every complaint. A client asking for one at 2330 before surgery may be anxious. Ask about the cause first.

Before any sedative, check breathing and recent opioids. Hold the sedative if breathing is already slow or shallow, and report it. Breathing pauses with low oxygen after an opioid outrank other sleep needs.

A client who cannot be awakened is not just in deep sleep. Assess right away for causes such as low blood sugar.

New confusion after a sedative is an adverse effect. Keep the client safe, assess, and report. Do not give more sedation or use restraints as the answer. New confusion in a post-op client also needs a search for a physical cause.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Do not mistake time in bed for sleep, aging for disease, or a dangerous change for tiredness.
sections.source: Module 7 slides 63, 66–67; other rows added for the NCLEX
sections.body: These look-alike ideas often show up as wrong answers.

rows: Eight hours in bed can include many awakenings.
Earlier, lighter sleep is normal. Breathing pauses and disabling sleepiness are not.
A client who cannot be awakened needs immediate assessment.
Group nonurgent tasks. Keep all required checks.
Treat pain, anxiety, or noise first.
A night-shift worker may have a normal pattern for them.
Alcohol helps onset but breaks up later sleep.
Current staging is N1, N2, N3.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Assess before sedating, and treat any change in alertness or breathing as the priority.
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials
sections.body:
Expect priority items about overnight rounds, sedative safety, and age norms. Select-all items ask about sleep assessment questions or safe interventions.

Sample question: A hospitalized client asks for a sleeping pill after waking many times. The client reports pain at 8/10 and loud hallway noise. What should the nurse do first?
steps: Read the stem: repeated waking, pain 8/10, and hallway noise.
What is it really asking? Should you treat the causes or just sedate?
Key cues: Severe pain and noise are clear, fixable causes.
Wrong options: Requesting sedation and rechecking pain tomorrow leaves severe pain untreated. Starting a diary before fixing the room delays help. Encouraging daytime naps can worsen night sleep.
The answer: Assess the pain, give indicated relief, and reduce the avoidable noise.
Strategy: Look for a cause in the stem and target it before choosing medication.

sections.heading: Worked case: broken sleep and failed teaching
sections.keyIdea: Poor learning after a bad night is a clue to assess sleep, not proof of poor effort.
sections.source: Added: worked example based on Module 7 slides 66–68
sections.body:
Mr. T is awake much of the night from pain, frequent toileting, and hallway noise. In the morning he is irritable and cannot focus on new teaching. The chart says “poor participation.” That note does not explain why.

First rule out urgent causes. New confusion or low responsiveness needs assessment, not a sleep hygiene talk.

Then target each cause. Do not assume one sedative will fix several untreated problems. Do not assume all older adults sleep poorly.
steps: Describe his sleep and his alertness now. Is this new?
Find causes: pain, toileting, noise, medicines, and worry.
Treat pain, help with safe toileting, and reduce avoidable noise.
Cluster nonurgent care while keeping required checks.
Reteach when he is alert, and ask him to explain it back in his own words.

check.q: Why is “client stayed in bed all night” not enough evidence that the plan worked?
check.a: It does not show actual sleep, fewer awakenings, restfulness, or daytime function. He may have been awake, in pain, or oversedated.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.source: Module 7 slides 59–68 (course notes and clarifications)
sections.body: Use these notes to connect the lesson with your course materials.
bullets: Source: Module 7, Exemplar 7.C, slides 59–68.
The slides use an older four-stage NREM scheme with N3 and N4. Current staging (NHLBI) combines them into N3, for three NREM stages.
The slides give approximate cycle length, timing, and percentages. Cycles vary by person.
The slide lists “↓ serotonin and GABA → promote sleep.” That is misleading. GABA activity supports sleep pathways.
The course says infants sleep through the night by 6 months. Individual babies vary.
Sedative safety and danger signs are added for the NCLEX.

pearls: Hours in bed do not equal hours asleep.
Assess quality, quantity, continuity, and daytime function.
Older adults still need restful sleep.
Cluster nonurgent care while keeping required monitoring.
Check breathing and recent opioids before any sedative.
Bright days and dark nights help reset a disrupted body clock.
redFlags: A client who is newly hard to arouse, acutely confused, or breathing poorly needs prompt assessment.
Breathing pauses with marked daytime sleepiness need follow-up.
Breathing pauses with low oxygen after an opioid are a priority.
New sedation, falls, or confusion after a medicine need reassessment and a report.

checks.q: A client says, “I’m in bed eight hours, but I wake every hour and can’t concentrate.” What does this show?
checks.a: Time in bed is not the same as good sleep. The sleep is broken and is affecting daytime function.

checks.q: How many NREM stages are used today?
checks.a: Three: N1, N2, and N3. The older N3 and N4 stages are now combined as N3.

checks.q: A UAP plans to skip the 0400 vital signs because the client finally fell asleep. What should the nurse say?
checks.a: Required monitoring cannot be skipped. Do it quietly and cluster other nonurgent care.

checks.q: A 79-year-old goes to bed at 2030, wakes at 0430, and feels rested. Is this a problem?
checks.a: Probably not. Earlier sleep timing is common with aging. Judge by total sleep and daytime function.

checks.q: What comes before a request for routine sedation?
checks.a: Assess the sleep pattern and causes, including pain, breathing, anxiety, medicines, substances, and environment.
